title: Independent Feedback Loops
author: Craig Latimir
summary: Craig Latimir uses a blindfolded-archery analogy to define 'independent feedback loops' -- situations where a learner can adjust their practice using near-instant feedback with no expert input required. Practical subjects like tennis serves or art techniques have this built in naturally; academic subjects like maths, history, or writing typically don't, meaning students can practice a skill incorrectly for an entire session before finding out. For subjects with a single correct answer, Latimir recommends sharing answers alongside questions rather than waiting until the end, pairing this with backwards-faded worked examples, and building explicit self-checking steps into the task itself. For open-response subjects, he recommends clear, sequenced success criteria and mid-task exposure to examples and non-examples so students can self-assess before time runs out.
points: Latimir's core distinction: an 'independent feedback loop' lets a learner act on feedback instantly with no expert input needed -- true of practical skills like a tennis serve, but rarely true of academic tasks like solving equations or writing an essay.

For subjects with a single correct answer, his key recommendation is not waiting until the end of practice to share answers, since letting students practice a wrong method for an entire session 'at best was a waste and at worst has helped embed some misconceptions.'
Backwards-faded worked examples, combined with early answer-sharing, let students pinpoint the exact step where their understanding breaks down rather than only knowing the final answer was wrong.

For open-response subjects without a single right answer, his fix is clear, sequenced success criteria plus mid-task exposure to examples and non-examples, so students can self-assess before time is up.
quotes: Let's call scenario A an 'independent feedback loop'. This is where the user receives feedback which they can act upon instantly with no direct input from another expert needed.
For those who got some or most wrong, their time spent practising at best was a waste and at worst has helped embed some misconceptions which might move learning backwards for them.

If the problems require multiple steps to complete then, by using backwards faded examples which add an extra step as the questions develop, combined with answers being shared, leaners will be able to pinpoint the exact step at which they have a gap in their learning.
Giving learners explicit success criteria to hit at specific points can help them self-assess their work.
Let us not forget that there is also plenty that can be done, through careful thought and task design, to ensure that time spent practising is always time well spent.
